speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for the results; the negative Coombs test and normal ultrasound help rule out hemolytic disease and structural issues like biliary atresia. Since your bilirubin is elevated but indirect, were you breastfed exclusively, and do you have any siblings who experienced jaundice as newborns? This will help distinguish between breast milk jaundice or physiological jaundice versus other causes.

speaker: Patient
text: 5-day-old male newborn. The newborn's mother reports that her child has developed yellowish discoloration of the skin that started from the face and then spread to the trunk since the past day. There have been no changes in his bowel habits or urination. The baby was born full-term at 38 weeks’ gestation via an uncomplicated vaginal delivery and has been exclusively breastfed every 2–3 hours.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Physiological Jaundice of the Newborn. The clinical presentation of yellowing starting on day 5, spreading from face to trunk, combined with a full-term birth, negative Coombs test, normal ultrasound, and exclusive breastfeeding, is classic for physiological jaundice. Continued monitoring of bilirubin levels is recommended to ensure they do not rise to dangerous levels requiring phototherapy.
